chung.Time Allocation:
Study hour (150h) = 45 contact hours (60 sessions) + 104 hours of self-study + 1 hour for the final exam
1 session = 45 minutes
chung.Description: The course is designed to consolidate and enhance students' grammatical knowledge. It aims to achieve this by giving learners exposure to grammar as it is used in real life situations, offering them comprehensive explanations for grammatical forms and meanings, providing contextualized practice of various structures, and developing their use of such structures as well as their critical thinking skills through communicative activities. Students will also be informed of how to recognize common grammatical errors in their written work and encouraged to apply learned grammar in writing. Utilizing a flipped classroom approach, they will engage with core grammar concepts and materials independently before class sessions. They are also encouraged to leverage AI tools as resources to support their grammar learning, practice, and writing processes.

- From week 3, students work in groups of 5 to:
+ Choose 2 units from the units taught in the course.
+ Conduct peer-teaching sessions. For these sessions, they prepare interactive activities to help their classmates review and practice the grammatical structures from the Grammar Notes section of these units .

Suggested Peer-Teaching Activities:
+ Grammar quizzes or “Find the error” challenges
+ Role-plays or dialogues using the target structure
+ Mini grammar games (e.g., Kahoot, Jeopardy, sentence race)
+ Sentence-combining or transformation tasks
+ Short group writing or storytelling using the grammar point
+ Peer-correction or editing activities

*Students are encouraged to use AI tools to assist with this project. Any use of AI tools must be clearly documented in the project report submitted to the lecturer. Potential uses include:
+ Generate examples for the target grammar point
+ Create quiz items, dialogues, or game questions
+ Get feedback on lesson plans or activity instructions
+ Other purposes

Instructions and schedules for the mini project must be presented in the course implementation plan approved by the head of the department.

Instructors are responsible for informing students about the project at the beginning of the course and reviewing them after grading.

*Option 1:
Students work in a group of 5:
- Each group contacts lecturers of ENT/TRS classes, BEN's writing classes (EAW, ERW, ENB) or ENM classes to ask for 3 pieces of writing (paragraphs, essays or emails) in which grammatical errors are largely present.
- Each member in a group is in charge of identifying any grammatical errors in the 3 pieces of writing obtained.
- Each group writes a booklet for EFL learners. In the booklet, they select the most common grammatical errors (at least 5) from the pieces of writing, put forward suggestions on how to avoid them, and design some exercises to help the readers practice writing sentences/paragraphs with the relevant grammatical structures.
- The groups send their booklets to the lecturer in charge for marking and give a presentation on how they have worked on the booklet in class for feedback.
- The lecturer in charge can invite other lecturers to come to the class, and the groups can pitch the booklet to them.

*Students are encouraged to use AI tools to assist with this project. Any use of AI tools must be clearly documented in the project report submitted to the lecturer. Potential uses include:
+ Error Identification: Students can first identify grammatical errors manually and then use AI tools to perform the same task. This allows them to compare their own findings with the AI's suggestions.
+ Researching Explanations: They can use AI tools to find reliable materials that come with grammatical explanations, which will help them write the section on how to avoid common errors.
+ Designing Exercises: They can use AI tools to generate draft exercises for the booklet, which they must then review and adjust for suitability and accuracy.
+ Other Purposes.

*Option 2: Lecturer’s choice

These activities can be performed throughout Weeks 1–2 so that students can achieve the AI-integration learning outcome by Session 12:
- Compare and contrast AI’s explanations to advanced grammatical structures when using different prompting techniques
- Compare and contrast AI’s examples when using different prompting techniques

Suggested prompting techniques for the activities:
+ Zero-shot prompting: Give AI a direct, no-example request.
+ Few-shot prompting: Provide a few examples within the prompt to guide AI on the desired format or style.
+ One-shot prompting: A specific type of few-shot prompting where only one example is given.
+ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting: Break down complex problems into smaller, sequential steps to guide the model through a logical process.
+ Contextual prompting: Provide extra background information and details to improve AI's understanding.
